notes.word: have with this meaning is a stative (non-action) verb and is not used in continuous tenses.
notes.example: I have a car, but I don't say 'I am having a car.'
notes.source_text: I have a car, but I don't say 'I am having a car.'

notes.word: She has three brothers and a close relationship with her cousins.
notes.example: He has a serious illness that requires regular treatment.
notes.source_text: He has a serious illness that requires regular treatment.

notes.word: have with this meaning is a dynamic (action) verb and can be used in continuous tenses.
notes.example: She is having a meeting with her team right now.
notes.source_text: She is having a meeting with her team right now.

notes.word: I had the mechanic fix my car yesterday.
notes.example: She had her house painted last summer because it was looking old.
notes.source_text: She had her house painted last summer because it was looking old.

notes.word: In negative sentences, we occasionally leave out got, especially in fixed expressions like I haven't time, I haven't a clue.
notes.example: I haven't a clue where she went, but we can ask around.
notes.source_text: I haven't a clue where she went, but we can ask around.

notes.word: have got to is normally used for a specific obligation rather than a general or repeated obligation.
notes.example: I have got to finish this report by 5 PM today, so I can’t go out now.
notes.source_text: I have got to finish this report by 5 PM today, so I can’t go out now.

notes.word: I have to wear a suit to work. (= general)

notes.source_text: At my office, I have to wear a suit to work every day.

notes.word: I've got to make a quick phone call. (= specific)
notes.example: I've got to finish this report before the meeting starts.

notes.word: I have been studying English for three years.

notes.word: We also use have for other perfect forms, e.g. the future perfect, the perfect infinitive, the past perfect, etc.
notes.example: By next week, she will have finished the report. (future perfect) He seems to have missed the meeting. (perfect infinitive) They had already left when I arrived. (past perfect)
notes.source_text: By next week, she will have finished the report. (future perfect) He seems to have missed the meeting. (perfect infinitive) They had already left when I arrived. (past perfect)
